A MURDEROUS ASSAULT.
Mr Wilkins at the Point of Death---Attacked by a Drunken Negro,
(Special to News and Observer.)

Roxboro, N. C., Nov. 9.—A negro named Adam Hunt made a murderous and probably fatal assault on Mr. Fleet Wilkins, a merchant living near Roxboro.

The negro was in the employment of R. W. Massic & Co., at their saw mill, and Mr. Wilkins' brother, who was absent, is book-keeper and cashier for Massic. The negro came into the store of Mr. Wilkin and demanded money. He was given a dollar and told the remainder, if any due, would be paid by the cashier on his return.

The negro returned in a short while in a drunken condition and demanded money. Mr. Wilkins again explained and refused, whereupon the negro struck him, crushing in the side of his head and driving the teeth and jaw into the roof of his mouth.

The negro continued to assault his helpless victim, when Mrs. Wilkins, who was present, got a pistol and attempted to shoot Hunt, but the pistol was unloaded and the negro ran her for some distance.

A Mr. Singleton coming up at that moment was assaulted and knocked down. The negro was quickly captured by a posse and is now in jail. Mr. Wilkins, who is a very frail man, has never regained consciousness and is reported to be in a dying condition tonight.

ATTEMPT TO LYNCH.
The Mob Demanded Keys of Sheriff Thompson.
He Did Not Have Them, and Those Who Would Have Lynched Adam Hunt Left Without Him.
(Special to News and Observer.)

Durham, N. C., Nov. 16.—An attempt was made at Roxboro last evening to lynch Adam Hunt, the negro who killed the young man Wilkins a few days ago. Mr. L. J. Winstead, a young man who lives at Winstead but had been to Roxboro on a visit, said that soon after midnight a party of some fifty men went to the home of Sheriff Thompson and demanded the keys to the jail. He had previously let one of his deputies have the keys and he was finally able to convince the crowd that he did not have any access to the jail.

After this the crowd left but were expected to come back again later in the night. In the meantime Congressman W. W. Kitchin, who was spending a day or so at home, Hon. J. A. Long and a few others assembled to be present when the crowd came back and use their influence to prevent a lynching in the county. Their services were not needed, however, as they did not come back after the negro.

Judge O. H. Allen spent last night in the city and left this morning for Roxboro where he is holding court this week. It is supposed that the negro will be placed on trial at once and it is generally thought that this fact will prevent any further attempt to end the life of the negro. The negro says that he had no idea he would kill Mr. Wilkins, but it is said that the State has evidence that Hunt remarked on the day of the killing that there would be a dead man in that settlement before night.

ADAM HUNT ON TRIAL.
The Mob Had No Leader, Elsa He Would Hava Been Lynched.
(Special to News and Observer.)

(Special to News and Observer.)

Durham, N. C., Nov. 17.—Adam Hunt, the negro who a few days ago killed the young man named Wilkins near Roxboro, spent a part of last night in Durham county jail and was taken back to Roxboro. He was brought over here on the late Norfok and Western train for safe keeping over night. He was carried back this morning and the trial was on today.

On Sunday night there was an unsuccessful attempt to lynch the negro, a crowd of some forty or fifty men making an effort to get hold of the keys. Court convened yesterday, and in order to be sure that the negro was not killed without a trial he was brought over here by two deputies. Very few people knew that he was in Durham until this morning.

Regarding the attempt to lynch on Sunday night it is said that the only reason there was not a lynching was because the would-be lynchers did not have a leader. They did all they could to get a man to lead the party, but could not find one. Finally the crowd that had assembled moved on to the home of the sheriff and the lynching would have occurred anyway if they could have secured the keys. But when this failed there was no one to lead the party in a storm on the jail.

NRCHINA, VA. Nov. 24--Willi

(Virgilina, VA., Nov. 24.—William Cosby shot a white man near Houston, Va., November 4th. The owner of a certain tract of land caught Cosby hunting on his premises and ordered him off. The reply was a load of shot, which inflicted a serious wound in the owner's foot. William took French leave, but as this was not his first offense, Sheriff T. R. Jordan, of Halifax, made a special effort to catch his man. He succeeded in locating him in Oxford, N. C., and wired the chief of police there to arrest and hold him, which was done. James Wrenn, the Oxford chief of police, upon receipt of the necessary requisition papers, agreed to deliver his prisoner to Sheriff Jordan at this place at 1 o'clock Sunday, and his carriage had just crossed the North Carolina line when the negro, though handcuffed, jumped from the carriage and made a break for liberty.

The officers tried to stop him, and fired some shots to scare him, but he did not mind that, until finally the officers succeeded in sending a 44-calliber bullet through the fleshy part of his leg. Dr. P. P. Causey declared the wound was painful, but not serious. After Sheriff Jordan had the wound dressed he handcuffed his prisoner to the buggy and left for Houston, where Halifax court is in session.

Adam Hunt, who brutally murdered Fleetwood Wilkins near Roxboro last Saturday, two weeks ago, was indicted last Tuesday in Person County Court, tried on Wednesday, found guilty and sentenced to be hanged thirty days from that day.

This is the kind of justice to prevent lynching.

The State wins in the Supreme Court against the Armour Packing Company. The opinion came down yesterday in the case of Lacy vs. Packing Company, from Buncombe, and it said "no error." The court's opinion was unanimous, and was written by Chief Justice Walter Clark.

This case was argued on appeal last November, coming up from the Buncombe Superior Court. Messrs. Pou & Fuller, of this city, and T. B. Felder, of Atlanta, appeared for the packing company, and Attorney General R. D. Gilmer for the State.

The suit involved the constitutionality of section 56 of the Revenue Act of 1903, imposing a tax upon meat packing houses of $100 for each county in which the business is carried on. The Armour Packing Company has cold storage plants at five places in North Carolina, Wilmington, Greensboro, Asheville, Charlotte and Fayetteville. It ships to those points the products of its plant, and they remain there in cold storage till disposed of in due course of trade. The company maintains at those points bookkeepers, stenographers, salesmen, shipping clerks, drivers, etc.

It was contended by the company that it was not engaged in doing a packing house business in North Carolina, and that the tax was an interference with interstate commerce and a violation of the provisions of the State Constitution relating to taxation by uniform rule. The court in the opinion holds under the facts agreed that the Armour Packing Company is doing business in North Carolina, and that it is competent for the Legislature to prescribe such conditions as it may see fit, in order that corporations may do business within the State. It is further held that the tax applies to inter-State business, and that inter-State business is not affected by it. The court overrules the contention of the defendant company that the tax violates the rule of uniformity, holding that a tax is uniform when it bears equally upon all persons belonging to the described class upon which it is imposed, and that the Legislature is the sole judge of what subjects it shall select for such taxation, and that in the exercise of its discretion it is not subject to approval of the judicial department of the State.

DURHAM RADS MEET ON 30TH.
Adam Hunt Would as Lief Die One Time as Another.
(Special to News and Observer.)

Durham, N. C., April 13.—The County Republican Convention has been called to meet at noon on April 30th, this convention being for the purpose of electing delegates and alternates to the State Convention in Greensboro.

Another convention will be held later at which time the question of a county ticket will be decided. It is understood that a straight ticket will be put in the field. The outlook now is that the fight here this year will be a warm one between the two parties.

Adam Hunt, the condemned negro murderer, who was brought here from Person county to keep him out of a mob's hands, is still in the county jail. He faces death ecolly and says that he had just as well die now as to wait a few years longer. It will be remembered that Hunt killed a white man by the name of Fleet Wilkins, beating him in a horrible and unmerciful manner, death following in a short while. After his conviction in the Superior Court of Person county and an appeal was taken to the Supreme Court, there was a demonstration against Hunt's life and he was brought here. Since then the Supreme Court has affirmed the decision of the lower court and it is now up to the Governor to name the day on which he is to die. He will be kept here until the time for his execution and will then be taken to Person county.

The authorities are making every preparation to begin the arrest of those who refuse vaccination. The time limit expires tomorrow and this morning Mayor Freeland was out in a card in the morning paper saying that the law would certainly be enforced upon all alike. In the meantime Chief of Police J. A. Woodall is busy filling out warrants, leaving blank space for the names of the defendants.

In Person County Superior Court the case of Lee against the Seaboard Air Line has been settled. This suit was for $25,000 on account of the killing of young Sidney Lee on the yard of the road here. He received nominal damages in the compromise.

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

ROXBORO, N. C., June 15.—Adam Hunt, the murderer of Fleet Wilkins, was hanged here to-day with a hitch. Fourteen minutes after drop fell, he was pronounced dead by the physicians in charge, thus ending the life of a most desperate negro. There was a sigh of relief when it was known that it was over, and gratifying to all law-abiding citizens that the law had been allowed to take its course, and that mob violence had not been resorted to.

Fleet Wilkins, a young white man, who was his victim, was the proprietor of a store, just two miles from Rodxboro, at a saw-mill. This negro, under the influence of liquor, went to the store and demanded the money, which was due him. He was told by Wilkins that his brother had the account, and that he had gone to Lynchburg for the day, and, not knowing what was due the negro, refused to pay all the negro demanded. A fight ensued, and the negro being a very powerful one, soon had the life most beat out of young Wilkins. By some means Wilkins got out of the store and staggered along home. Hunt overtook him and killed him, almost at his own door, literally crushing the life out of him, breaking nearly every bone in the young man's body, and horribly mutilating him. There was a stubborn fight put up to save the negro's life, but of no avail, the Governor, refusing to commute his sentence.

WITH BULLETS NEGRO'S BODY RIDDLED BY MOB IN JAIL. SHERIFF OFFERS RESISTANCE. He and His Guard Wounded One of the Mob and Captured Three More.
Nashville, Tenn., Sept. 25.—A special from Lynchburg, Tenn., to the Banner says a negro was killed and a member of a mob wounded in an assault on the jail last night. A crowd of about twenty-five reached the jail shortly before midnight and demanded the keys to the cell in which Allen Small, a negro, was incarcerated. Sheriff G. B. Davidson had no intimation of any contemplated violence and was alone at the time. He peremptorily refused to accede to the demand and immediately opened fire on the would-be lynchers and succeeded in wounding one of them who was taken off by his friends. His identity and the extent of his injuries cannot be learned.

At the same time the Sheriff called the police for assistance. Two of the police and several citizens rushed to the jail, but before they arrived the mob had succeeded in battering down the wooden door at the foot of the stairs leading to the corridor. The Sheriff and his posse made a stout resistance, but were unable to prevent the mob from breaking in the iron door at the head of the stairs and entering the cell occupied by the negro, about whose neck they placed a rope.

As soon as the men emerged from the cell it became apparent that the negro could not be taken from the jail and hung, and he was shot and instantly killed. The mob then made an effort to escape, but the Sheriff and his guard succeeded in holding three of them, and they are now in jail on the charge of murder. The men are Dock Hasty, his brother and John Dean, and one of them has made a confession implicating thirteen men in the raid.

The grand jury at Lynchburg, Tenn., has returned a verdict that the negro Allen Small, who was killed Thursday night, Sept. 24, in a raid on the Monroe county jail, was deliberately murdered, and twenty-seven men are named in the indictments as guilty of the crime.

Fourteen of the men said to have been in the mob are under arrest and warrants for the others have been issued. Three of the prisoners have turned state's evidence, and have been released on bond on condition that thy will appear as witnesses for the prosecution when the cases are called.

Minneapolis
POLICE GET ORDERS TO STOP RACE WAR Prompt Arrests Will Follow Further Negro Beating in Minneapolis.
The police of Minneapolis are under instructions to immediately and forcibly suppress demonstrations against colored men, of which there have been several more or less aggravated instances during the last few days.

Last night Charles Collins, a St. Paul colored man employed as porter in a saloon at Washington and Hennepin, was assaulted by two unknown white men and badly bruised. There would have been a cutting affray but for the white wife of the assaulted man, who clung about his neck and was largely instrumental in preventing his use of the knife he carried.

On Thursday night a similar case of assault occurred, when two colored men were observed eating ice cream in a candy store at Third street and First avenue. Several white men assaulted the blacks, and the fight was stopped by a police officer.

The colored men who have married white women are much excited over these apparent indications of public feeling against them, and there have been several meetings of the class referred to with the object of deciding how they shall behave if attacked.

It develops that more than half of the colored waiters at the West hotel have white wives, and the same or a greater percentage exists among black waiters in nearly all the cafes and hotels of Minneapolis and St. Paul. The women who have married black men declare in the majority of cases that they are satisfied with their selections and have no complaints to make. Most of them appear anxious lest there should be further exhibitions of animosity against colored husbands of white wives, and insist that the matter of their husband's color is one that concerns the wives rather than the public.

"I have been married to my husband for eight years," said one white woman last night. "I am of Swedish parentage. I married my husband because I loved him. He has been always thoughtful of me, an excellent provider for his family, kind, good hearted to an excess, and in every way a good husband. He has never been intoxicated, he brings me every dollar he earns, we are building a little home of our own and if people mind their own business we shall always be happy together. We have children and I love them none the less because they are brown instead of white."

"The colored men in Minnesota are well behaved and hard working as a class. There are some worthless characters among them, but certainly not a greater proportion than would be found among the same number of whites. It seems to me an outrage that a few drunken rowdies who are down town at night when they ought to be in their homes, should be allowed to interfere with other men in every way respectable and hard working citizens, simply because they are black."

The dictum of Superintendent Conroy of the Minneapolis police department is that every person of whatever color who creates a disturbance on the street is to be promptly arrested and locked up. It has come to the attention of the police that a sort of feud has arisen within the last week or two between a certain class of whites and that class of colored people whose employment keeps them down town all night. The department is determined to suppress any tendency toward negro baiting in Minneapolis and persons suspected of such tendencies are being closely watched.

LYNCHED FOR MURDER.
Negro Was Charged with Killing Confederate Veteran.
[ BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE. ]
mbia S. C. July 1 — Charles Eva

Columbia, S. C., July 1.—Charles Evans was taken out of a shanty guardhouse at Norway, Orangeburg County, early this morning, and hanged. He was arrested yesterday, suspected of having assassinated James T. Phillips the night before. Phillips, a Confederate veteran, the father of nineteen children, was shot in the head at his supper table, two children being wounded by the same shot. The villagers tracked the assassins, there were two, and caught Charles Evans.

Late in the evening a message was received that Henry Evans, a brother of Charles, was on the outskirts of the town, and for the whites to get him. On repairing to the place the white men found twelve armed negroes waiting for a fight, but they were overpowered and three were locked up. Later these men were taken out and beaten. All declared that the Evanses shot Phillips. After being whipped the men were released and Charles Evans was hanged. Henry Evans surrendered to the Sheriff in Orangeburg this evening.

Governor Heyward telegraphed both Sheriff and coroner to take the most vigorous action in hunting down the lynchers and to call on him for any assistance needed.

SOUTH CAROLINA LYNCHING.
Alleged Murderer is Strung Up by a Mob.
Columbia, S. C., July 1.—Governor Heyward this morning received a telegram from Norway, fifty miles south of Columbia, on the Seaboard Railroad, announcing that Charley Evans, the suspected murdered of John T. Phillips, had been taken from the guard house last night and lynched. Governor Heyward immediately wired Sheriff Dukes, of Orangeburg, to protect any other prisoners under arrest, and to do everything possible to apprehend the lynchers.

The killing of Mr. Phillips was a horrible crime. He was seated at his supper table Monday night when he was shot in the back of the head.

Two of his little children were also struck by shot.

It seems that an uprising of the negroes was feared, for merchants in this city received dispatches from white people in Norway asking for twenty-five rifles.

Phillips's son had whipped some negroes at Norway Saturday afternoon, and this started the feeling which led to the homicide. Charley Evans was the mulatto son of a white man, and as soon as the homicide occurred suspicion was directed at him. His brother is also implicated by Evans' confession.

Four negroes who had been arrested and were in the guard-house with Evans were taken out and whipped into insensibility.

If Evans' brother is captured he will be lynched in all probability. John T. Phillips was a one-armed Confederate soldier. This is the first lynching under Governor Heyward's administration.

TROUBLE AT NORWAY.
Columbia Militia Sent to Suppress Threatening Uprising of Negroes.

Fifty Columbia militiamen went to Norway, Orangeburg county last Saturday night to protect the town from a threatening attack by a large crowd of Negroes.

During Saturday afternoon the following dispatch was received in Columbia from J. L. Glover, mayor of Norway: "Governor D. C. Heyward, Columbia: Send troops to Norway at once. Trouble expected."

Telephonic conversation between the authorities in Columbia and Mayor Glover, developed the fact that the Negroes in the vicinity of Norway were very much wrought up over the lynching of Charles Evans for the assassination of Mr. John Phillipps, and that they were gathering in force for the purpose of making an attack on the town.

Governor Heyward was not in Columbia, having been called out of town on business; but Gen. Frost, Attorney General Gunter and Col. Willie Jones took charge of the situation, and decided that a company of fifty men should be sent.

It was after 11 o'clock p. m., when the telegram was received from Mayor Glover; but it happened that all of the Columbia companies were within comparatively easy reach. They were in attendance on a military entertainment at Hyatt Park, three miles from the city. Gen. Frost called for an officer over the telephone and the first one with whom he got into communication was Capt. L. W. Haskell. Capt. Haskell grasped the situation at once and the only trouble he had was holding the number down to fifty men as fully 150 were anxious to go. However, he took detachments from all three of the Columbia companies including commissioned officers who volunteered to go in the ranks as privates.

By 12.30 p. m., the men were in their armory, provided with ammunition and ready for business. In the meantime a special train had been procured from the Seaboard Air Line road, and at 12.50 o'clock the train pulled out for Norway, making the entire trip of 42 miles in 48 minutes.

On the arrival of the troops at Norway, it developed that several hundred Negroes had collected during the day at a place called Bush Pond, about three miles distant, and that they had been threatening to kill B. S. Hutto, G.. F. Toole, Pete Gibson. Launcy Young and Henry Dukes, all of whom were alleged to have been connected with the lynching of the Evans Negro. About fifteen Norway men were standing guard at the Hutto farm, awaiting an attack.

The feeling and understanding was that it was the purpose of the Negroes to attack after the moon went down, or shortly before daylight. The soldiers kept on the alert; but were unable to see anything of an especially suspicious nature, and the next day they decided to return to Columbia, arriving there at 1 o'clock p. m.

Old man John T. Phillips, who had been fired on from ambush by the Evans Negro, about six days before, died Sunday morning at 6.50 o'clock. He had been wounded by five buckshot, and at least two of the shots were calculated to produce death.

Mr. Phillips left a large family, including grown sons, and in view of the general situation it is quite possible that there may be trouble yet. Sheriff Dukes, of Orangeburg had arrived at Norway before the departure of the troops and it was thought that he could preserve order at least as long as he might remain on the ground.

CORONER'S INQUEST HELD
IN THE LYNCHING CASE.
Witnesses Examined---The Verdict Was That Evans Died at Hands of Unknown Parties
Special to The State.

Special to The State.
Norway, July 2.—An inquest over the body of Chas. Evans, who was lynched here Tuesday night. was held this morning by Coroner Rickenbacker. Six witness were examined. The first witness, Dr C. H. Ables, testified, as follows: "About 8 o'elock yesterday morning I was driving out of town when I saw a dead body hanging to a tree about one mile out of town, and about 100 yards from the road. I went up to see what I could learn. I found that it was the body of Chas. Evans and saw many gunshot wounds in the body. I heard no shooting the night before. I saw strangers in town but heard nothing that would lead me to think there would be anything done Monday night."

The second witness, Mr. B. S. Cogburn, testified, as follows: "I was asleep Tuesday night at home when I was awakened during the night by the firing of guns and as the firing ceased I did not go out to see where it was. After I arose next morning and went to my place of business I heard that a negro had been lynched out of town, and with others I went out to where the body was hanging to an oak tree by a rope around the neck and the hands tied behind the back. I did not know who the negro was. I had never seen him before. I saw a great many strangers in town the evening before, but did not hear any one say anything about lynching a negro that night."

Other witnesses examined testified about the same thing and after a short talk to the jury by Coroner Rickenbacker the jury came to a verdict "that the deceased came to his death from the effect of gun who the effect of gun shots and strangulation at the hands of a party or parties unknown to the jury."

Everything is quiet again. No more trouble is expected from the negroes. The town was guarded well last night.

Mr. Phillips, who was shot on Monday night, is living, but it is not thought he will last through the night.

NEGRO SAVED FROM ATLANTA MOB.
[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]

Atlanta, Ga., July 13—Mrs. Susie Wells was attacked at her home in Central-st. this afternoon by Charles Lockett, a negro. Her screams attracted the attention of her sons, who came to her rescue. Lockett was overpowered by the young men after a hard fight. The affair soon became known throughout the city, and by the time the officers arrived a large crowd had collected about the house. There were many threats of lynching, but the patrolmen got the negro away by a back street and landed him safely in the Tower. It is believed that Lockett is partially insane.

Street.

A threatening crowd followed the negro and he in turn took refuge in a drug store where he was arrested.

Batiled With Police.
Andrew Crawford, a colored hotel porter, tried to hold up a hotel clerk in Parkersburg at the point of a revolver and demanded money from him. He was paid some money and went away. Officers were called and a running fight that lasted for several squares ensued. While still in the hotel the man fired at special constable Perry Nolan and constable Helmick. Nolan fired back, but the fellow escaped. Several police engaged in pursuit, and Crawford was finally brought to bay. He placed his revolver against Nolan's side and fired, but Nolan pushed the weapon down and it shot him in the foot. Then special policeman A. G. Davis fired, hitting the man in the back, paralyzing one side. After he was arrested he flourished his revolver and tried to shoot, but it was empty. It is probable he will die.

Whites Force Contractor to Allow Them to Choose Their Work.
Indianapolis, June 4.—Thirty negroes employed on the traction line of the Evansville and Princeton Company in Gibson county were driven from their work yesterday by whites, who claimed that the negroes were doing work that should be done by them. BREAKING OUT IN A NEW PLACE
The negroes have been bled by all sorts of schemes from the day of their emancipation until the present. Some of them in the long ago indulged in the luxury of badges of Lincoln and Grant, at so much per badge, coupled with the intimation that the presentation of that badge at almost any place was the open sesame to comfort and idleness. Many a poor negro parted with his dollar and found that he still had to work or come to grief.

Bright colored visions of a happy and easy life have been held out to them in "pastures green" of Liberia, and after paying the demands of some scheming scoundrel, they waked up to find a verification of the old adage, "A fool and his money is soon parted."

The Freedman's Bank which flourished for a while, under a nominal Federal supervision swallowed up many of the hard earned dollars of ignorant negroes.

The swindles practiced upon the ignorant negroes have been in every case of this sort, gotten up by their so called friends seeking to get them away from the South, the land of their birth and the home of their friends. Many and often have been the cases of Southern white men coming to their rescue when they had been tolled off and left stranded in distant places.

The latest proposition is for a negro invasion of Boston, some of the details of which are published in today's Advertiser. The Boston Post indicates that the work has been secret. God pity the negroes who go to Boston in great droves thinking to find employment or expecting to live in idleness. It will be the hardest proposition they ever ran up against. The misery they will suffer is beyond computation. The white people up there would make life for them one long horror, and it would not be a great while before they would be sighing for the Southern breezes and the rice and cotton fields of Dixie.

CORONER FOUND WOUNDS.
Man Found Dead at Oxford Was Cut With a Knife. Ansonia, Feb 24, Henry Bennet
Man Found Dead at Oxford Was Cut With a Knife.

Ansonia, Feb 24.—Henry Resnet, a Canadian woodchopper, was found dead early to-day amid the ruins of a little hut on land owned by John B. Pope of Oxford. Apparently the man had met his death while sleeping. Some marks, however, were noticed in the abdomen of the dead man which appeared to have been made by a knife which caused the authorities to call in the coroner, who made an investigation. Coroner Mix came from New Haven and after an examination of the body he found that a knife wound extended from the chest down into the abdomen so that the intetsines protruded. This looked like murder and it appeared to the authorities that the man had first been killed and his body placed on the bed, which was set on fire. An odor of kerosene was also discovered. From the peculiar circumstances connected with Resnet's death the authorities decided to arrest Fred Jackson, a negro of this city. Jackson said he slept with Resnet last night and as Jackson was not burned in any way it was believed he had committed the crime. He was locked up in the jail in Seymour. When searched a knife was found on him, the blade of which was moist, and this knife the coroner took with him to New Haven to have examined.

Jackson and Resnet formerly lived in the hut together, but recently they had quarreled and the colored man was ordered away. Yesterday Jackson returned and he had a talk with Resnet and after the conversation Jackson told Mr Pope that he and Resnet had patched up their difficulties and would work together again.

MAY BE FOUL PLAY. Authorities Investigating Death of Negro in Connecticut.
Ansonia, Ct., February 24.—Fred Jackson, a negro of this city, is held at the lockup, in Seymour, pending an investigation by the authorities of the cause of the death of Henry Resnet, a wood chopper, whose body burned to a crisp, was found about midnight last night, lying in the ruins of a little hut in Oxford where he lived. Coroner Mix of New Haven and Medical Examiner Barnes of Oxford, who examined the body this afternoon are said to have found a gash resembling a knife wound extending from the breast to the abdomen and of such depth that the intestines protruded.

There was an odor of kerosene, it is said, about the ruins of the hut. The theory on which the authorities are working is that Resnet was the victim of foul play and that his body was burned to conceal the crime.

Resnet was a French Canadian.

JACKSON'S STORY.
Man Who Is Held Pending Investigation of Resnet Death.
Man Who Is Held Pending Investigation of Resnet Death.

Seymour, Feb 25.—Fred Jackson, the negro who is held pending the investigation by the coroner of the death of Henry Resnet, whose body was found amid the ruins of his hut yesterday, made a statement to-day. He said that he slept in the hut that night and was awakened to find the place filled with smoke. Resnet he did not see until his body was carried from the ruins. He believes that a spark from Resnet's pipe set the swamp hay which was used for bedding on fire. Resnet, he said, was under the influence of liquor. He said he rushed out of the door as soon as he discovered the fire. The stains on the knife, he said, came from opening a can of tomatoes after the burning of the hut. Constable Hubbell, who was the first to reach the scene of the fire, said he had to burst the door in and he saw Resnet lying on the bed. He saw nothing of the negro Jackson.

THREATEN TO LYNCH NEGRO
French Canadian Woodchoppers Believe Jackson Murdered and Cremated Rasnet Near Oxford
Oxford, Conn., Feb. 26.—Uttering threats of lynching a gang of wood choppers most of them French Canadians, spent last night in searching the woods in this neighborhood for Fred Jackson, a negro, who was released from Seymour jail by order of the coroner after it had been decided that there was not sufficient evidence to warrant holding him on a murder charge. Jackson was a companion of Henry Resnet, a French Canadian whose body burned to a crisp was found Tuesday morning in the ruins of the hut he occupied.

On account of a suspicion of foul play Jackson was held pending the coroner's investigation and among friends of the dead man feeling against the negro ran high.

As soon as he was released from jail Jackson returned here and entered a barroom where he got into a quarrel with a number of wood choppers. In the brawl the negro was pummeled severely and might have suffered worse treatment had not the bartender interfered. The latter managed to get Jackson out of the room and told him to go into the woods as quickly as possible.

The wood choppers angry at Jackson's escape made threats against the bartender and had begun a search of the premises thinking the negro was concealed there when they learned that their man had taken to the woods. Derby, Conn., Feb. 26.—Vowing that they will have a negro's life, a dozen woodchoppers are searching the woods between this city and Oxford for Fred Jackson, a farmhand, who, they assert, murdered Henry Resnett, a fellow woodchopper, at Resnett's cabin, in Oxford. MOB'S VERDICT NOT SUSTAINED.
New-Haven, Conn., Feb. 27.—The report of Coroter Mix on the death of Henry Resnet, the woodchopper, whose burned body was found in the ruins of his hut in Oxford, was filed to-day. SHERIFF KEPT BACK OHIO MOB INTENT ON LYNCHING NEGROES. HE THREATENED TO SHOOT. If Mob Tried To Enter Jail—Excitement Subsides and Trouble Is Thought To Be Past.
Fremont, O., May 10.—Mob violence, which was threatened in this city last night as the result of the alleged killing of Otto Mischke by one of three negroes, subsided at 4 o'clock this morning. The three negroes who were charged with the crime are securely locked in the city jail at Norwalk, and the excitement that was rampant for several hours last night has about subsided.

From 1 o'clock until 4 Sunday morning the jail building was surrounded by an angry crowd, calling upon Sheriff Mason to deliver the prisoners. For an hour or more the Sheriff stood on the front steps of his residence and admonished the threatening crowd to be careful and quiet, and not commit an act that would forever shame Fremont in the eyes of the world. Sheriff Mason said he had taken an oath to do his official duty, and do it he would, and he said he would shoot the first man who made an attempt to break down the jail door and enter the building.

For fear of further trouble during the day and to-night, Mayor Engler ordered every saloon in the city closed.

The negroes gave their names as Wheeler Kimbro, Walter Stratton and Lorenzo Martin. Martin and Stratton had loaded revolvers in their possession.

To-day's story of the tragedy is to the effect that the negroes who were in the street were offended at a question of Mrs. Albert Gommell as to who they were. Mrs. Gommell was on her way home with her husband and children. Mischke, the victim, was living at the Gommell house, which was in the vicinity of the affray, and when he came to the door to see what the loud talk was about a bullet struck him in the stomach, inflicting a fatal wound.

MAYOR CALLED FOR TROOPS
But Gov. Nash Refused to Respond -- Situation at Fremont.
Columbus, May 13.—The state capital was thrown into excitement Tuesday night by news that a call had been made on Governor Nash for militia to quell trouble at Fremont, Sandusky county, where a big strike is in progress. The employers brought in negroes and Italians to break the strike and in a clash between these and unionists a striker named Otto Mischke was killed, which has intensified the bitterness and rendered the situation critical. The lives of the negroes and Italians are in danger and many are leaving the city. Mayor Engler communicated with Governor Nash and requested that troops be sent to Fremont, but as the situation had not then got beyond the control of local and county authorities, the governor refused to act. He instructed the mayor to follow the statutes, which give him power to call out troops located within the city of which he is mayor and judges authority to call out troops within their judicial district.

The mayor then applied to Major Myron C. Cox, commanding the third battalion of the Sixth infantry, O. N. G., of Fremont, for troops.

The mayor exceeded his authority in issuing this application and under the governor's ruling it counts for nothing. The mayor only has power to call for troops within his own city.

Adjutant General Gyger said last night that no instructions had been sent to any of the troops to be in readiness for a call and that none would be sent unless the sheriff of Sandusky was unable to handle the situation. This official claimed to be unable to secure deputies.

The colored strike breakers have been ordered to leave Fremont by the unionists and the police seem powerless to protect them. The Italians, who are few, have been given until Thursday to leave and as they are armed it is feared there will be blood-shed. While the situation is ominous enough in the eyes of the state's officials it has not yet reached the point where it is necessary to call out the troops.

So many conflicting stories have been sent broadcast over the country relative to the riot in Fremont, O., last Saturday night, resultant from a strike of the employees of the Clauss shear works, that it is about time for the truth to have a hearing. The facts are, that a number of Afro-Americans from Cleveland and other northern Ohio points were employed to take strikers' places. Some did not know that this was to be the case until almost on their arrival in Fremont. Others were made acquainted with the situation before arrival. As is usually the case, a mob consisting of strikers and sympathizers assaulted three young Afro-Americans by the names of Stratton, Kimbro and Martin, injuring severely at least one of them. They retaliated, shooting into the crowd and killing at least one striker and injuring others. This, of course, was in self-defense, because their lives were being jeopardized. As is usually the case, the Afro-Americans were arrested and taken to the jail at Norwalk, O., after a very weak attempt was made by two or three foolish admirers of the southern way of doing such things—lynching. They did not tarry long near the Fremont jail, because the sheriff told them in very plain language that he would kill anyone who approached any nearer the jail door. This, of course, settled the matter as far as the cowards were concerned. GIRL'S BODY IS FOUND
VICTIM OF AN UNKNOWN NEGRO'S CRIME NEAR LAWRENCEBURG.
She Was Not Ravished by Her Assailant, but Her Bones Were Broken by the Terrible Beating.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal. LAWRENCEBURG Ind.
LAWRENCEBURG, Ind., May 23.—The numerous posses which, day and night, have been scouring the country around Manchester Station in search of Rosa Kaiser, who was brutally assaulted, murdered and thrown into Tanner's creek Wednesday evening by an unknown negro who had previously beaten into insensibility and left for dead her father, seventy-three-year-old Martin Kaiser, were rewarded about 6 o'clock this morning by the finding of the girl's body in West Fork, a tributary of Tanner's creek, nearly three miles from the supposed scene of the tragedy.

The body, which lay close to the shore in a partly submerged clump of willows, was discovered by Leroy Clemm, a young man employed to look after the Big Four track lights along West Fork. All of the body save one hand was submerged, and it was this white hand on the surface of the water that attracted Clemm's attention.

Miss Kaiser evidently had been subjected to the most brutal and inhuman treatment. Her body was almost nude and bore unmistakable signs of the ravisher's work. The left arm was broken in two places and dislocated at the shoulder. There was a deep gash in her throat and her face was battered almost beyond recognition.

It was ascertained that the negro had kept his victim for some hours in a dismantled church about fifty yards from the junction of the West Fork and Tanner's creek. The interior of the church showed many indications of a terrible life-and-death struggle. There were numerous blood clots on the floor and walls. A blood-stained undergarment, identified as belonging to the murdered girl, was found near the crumbling altar.

The remains were taken to Guilford, Ind., on a handcar by section men and placed in the church to await the arrival of Coroner Swales, who was telegraphed for at once. Relatives arrived a few hours later and took charge of the body.

Martin Kaiser, father of the murdered girl, who came so near sharing, in a measure, her horrible fate, is expected to die at any moment. Mrs. Kaiser, who is confined to her bed with dropsy, suffered so severely from the effects of the shock that her life is despaired of.

Great excitement prevails in and about Manchester Station and the neighboring hamlets and a lynching or burning at the stake can scarcely be avoided if a suspect is captured and identified as the murderer in that locality. This morning this excitement assumed such a threatening aspect that it was deemed necessary to bring to this city for protection Louis Evenson, a negro suspect arrested at Cleves, O., last night and held there for identification. Accordingly, he was brought here about noon by Sheriff Axley and Marshal Jesse Crim, of Cleves, and placed in the county jail. Mrs. Mary Griffin and Mrs. Jane Darling, the two women who claim to have seen and talked with the supposed murderer a short time before the deed was committed, are expected to arrive here early to-morrow morning and identify Everson as the man who acted so suspiciously at their homes Wednesday afternoon. Everson is an exconvict. He is wanted at his home town, Rising Sun, Ind., for cutting with intent to kill. He is much feared in localities where he is well known.

When interviewed in his cell at the county jail this evening by a representative of the Journal, Everson admitted having passed through Manchester Station on the day of the murder, but emphatically denies any connection with the assault on either Mr. Kaiser or his daughter. Ever since his incarceration men from the remote country districts have been pouring into town and it is feared that a desperate effort will be made to lynch the negro. Sheriff Axley has placed a triple guard about the jail and every effort will be made to protect the prisoner from mob violence.

A post-mortem on the body of Rosa Kaiser develops the fact that she was not assaulted by her negro slayer, as was first supposed, evidently having perished in defense of her honor. Coroner Swaler, at the inquest this afternoon, rendered a verdict of "Murdered at the hands of some person or persons unknown, but believed to have been two negroes seen acting suspiciously near the scene of the crime shortly before the double assault was committed."

ANOTHER NEGRO WANTED
ATTEMPTED CRIMINAL ASSAULTS REPORTED IN DEARBORN.
The Perpetrator Escapes—Day of Excitement in and Around Lawrenceburg—Jail Heavily Guarded.
Associated Press Dispatch. LAWRENCEBURG.
LAWRENCEBURG, Ind., May 24.—This has been a day of intense agitation in the county over the murder of Rosa Kaiser and the murderous assault of her father last Wednesday night. Farmers gathered here, at Guilford, at Manchester and other towns in this county and openly threatened lynching if the guilty person could be identified. Sheriff Axby has a very strong guard of deputies at the jail to-night, where Louis Everson, known as "Black Ponto," is held on suspicion. There is no doubt that this negro would have been lynched to-day but for the announcement that Albert Darling, who came here from Manchester, did not identify him as the negro who called at the home of Mrs. Mary Griffin shortly before the assault on the Kaisers, and none of the other neighbors could identify the prisoner.

While the crowds were coming into town a dispatch was received that another outrage had been committed in the county and this diverted attention from the jail. Sheriff Axby, with deputies, was called to Weisburg, where an unknown negro, supposed to belong to the same railway construction gang, had criminally assaulted two little daughters of George Smith, a farmer. The sheriff was joined by many farmers in this chase and also by M. C. Cowdry, with his bloodhounds. After a hard chase it was found that the negro had boarded a freight train in the afternoon on the Big Four Railway at Sunman station, and when telegrams were sent after the train the negro could not be found. It is supposed he jumped off the train, possibly before it reached the next station, but he was on the cars long enough for the hounds to lose the trail.

Sheriff Axby, Deputy Patches and others returned to the jail here to-night, but the farmers, with the hounds, are still scouring the country. Sheriff Axby has a theory that the negro who escaped from Weisburg to-day is the one who assaulted the Kaiser family.

Mrs. Smith says she and her two little girls were alone in the house when the negro entered with a club. They screamed and escaped from the house and the negro fled in great haste before the neighbors reached them. Mrs. Smith's husband was taken to the asylum two weeks ago and it was known that she lived alone.

The funeral of Rosa Kaiser at Yorkville to-day was the most largely attended ever known in that vicinity and the feeling was intense. Neither of the parents could attend. The mother is a prostrated invalid and the father is still in a serious condition from his injuries.

John Frailor, of Seymour, was here tonight and identified the negro in jail as one who was in his meat store at Seymour the day following the Kaiser murder. The crowd had dispersed when this became known and all was quiet about the jail and in town, all the farmers being with the posses scouring the country for the Weisburg assailant. It was decided late tonight to take "Black Ponto" to Rising Sun for trial on an old charge of cutting to kill, and thus make sure of holding him, as it is believed that the prisoner is now at least implicated in the Kaiser tragedy.

NEGRO SUSPECT IS FREED
NO EVIDENCE OF HIS COMPLICITY IN ROSA KAISER'S MURDER.
Stoned and Cursed by a Mob as He Leaves Lawrenceburg—Reward for Murderers of Sutton and Yeager.
pecial to the Indianapolis Journal.
LAWRENCEBURG, Ind., May 25.—Louis Everson, alias Black Ponto, the negro held here for identification as the murderer of Rosa Kaiser, was escorted down the Big Four tracks beyond the city limits this evening by Sheriff Axby and Officers Petcher and Justis and told to make himself scarce, an order which he lost no time in obeying. He was followed for fully a mile by a hooting mob of men and boys, who cursed, stoned and beat him. He finally escaped, and was last seen entering a strip of woodland, where he is supposed to have sought concealment.

Although no incriminating evidence could be secured against Everson, there are many persons who still believe him to be guilty, and it is probable that he will be sought out and tarred and feathered, if no worse fate is meted out to him, unless he makes good use of his liberty.

The release of Black Ponto was occasioned by the receipt of a telephone message from the mayor of Rising Sun to the effect that the warrant issued for him in that city several months ago, had been withdrawn. The mayor added that the further Everson remained from Ohio county the better it would be for his safety, as he probably would be mobbed should he venture to return there so intense is the feeling against him.

The search for the negro suspect seen in Seymour on Friday night proved fruitless, as did the search for the negro who tried to assault the Schmidt children at Weisburg yesterday. The search for alleged white accomplices has been abandoned.

A petition requesting the contractors in charge of the Big Four improvements between Lawrenceburg Junction and Sunman's to dispense with colored labor, is being circulated by Louis Kaiser, brother of the murdered girl. The presence of so many negroes is regarded as a menace to the community and unless the contractors heed the request embodied in the petition it is believed that a war of extermination will be inaugurated against the blacks by the incensed friends of the murdered girl.

Physicians in attendance on Mr. and Mrs. Kaiser report that the aged couple are improving slowly, but are not yet out of danger.

MAY HAVE BEEN WHITE MAN.
New Theory Regarding the Kaiser Case at Lawrenceburg.
New Theory Regarding the Kaiser Case at Lawrenceburg.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

LAWRENCEBURG, Ind., May 26.—While the sheriff and deputies and many farmers are still scouring the country for the murderer of Rosa Kaiser, it is now believed that the assault on both Rosa and her father was by a white man and not by a negro, and that revenge instead of robbery was the motive. Martin Kaiser and Frank Aust, an uncle of Rosa Kaiser, are both of this opinion. Aust said to-day: "The man who did the deed is closer at home than any negro."

It also develops that Barney Schimes, a decrepit white inmate of the infirmary, who had wandered away, is the one who so badly frightened the Smith girls on Sunday while their mother and brother were at church, and in their fright, they aroused the neighborhood by saying a negro assaulted them.

Late to-night it was learned that an arrest in connection with the murder of Rosa Kaiser would probably be made to-morrow. It was said that a relative is under suspicion of having committee the deed, but the name of the accused could not be learned to-night.

Louis Everson, alias Black Ponto, the negro suspect released from the county jail here yesterday and stoned out of town, was arrested by Detective Jack Loftus at Dillsboro early this morning and returned here about 10 o'clock. He was at once released by Sheriff Axby and left on the run for the line.

SUSPECT IS HELD.
Negro Under Arrest for Alleged Murder of Indiana Girl Whose Body Was Found.
Lawrenceburg, Ind., May 25.—Louis Everson, a negro known as "Black Ponto," is in jail here on suspicion of having murdered Miss Rosa Kaiser, whose body was found in Tanner's creek Saturday. Her skull had been crushed and her face bruised and gashed.

Everson was placed in jail to protect him from mob violence. He denies that he had a hand in the girl's death or in the assault upon Martin Kaiser, the girl's father, who is still in a critical condition.

The tragedy has aroused the people, and every negro within five miles of Manchester has been ordered to leave at once.

John Frailer, of Seymour, was here Sunday night and identified the negro in jail as one who was in his meat store at Seymour the day following the Kaiser murder. The crowd had dispersed when this became known and all was quiet about the jail and in town all the farmers being with the posses scouring the country for the Weisburg assailant. It was decided to take "black Ponto" to Rising Sun for trial on an old charge of cutting to kill and thus make sure of holding him, as it is believed that the prisoner is now at least implicated in the Kaiser tragedy.

MURDER OF ROSA KAISER
DEARBORN COUNTY SHERIFF HOPE- FUL OF CLEARING UP CRIME.
Lawrenceburg Marshal Indulges in Some Sherlock Holmes Deductions— History of the Black Deed.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.
LAWRENCEBURG, Ind., Sept. 2.—Sheriff John Axby returned here to-day from Cincinnati, where, in conjunction with the police of that city, he has been making strenuous efforts to locate a young man named Otto Pool, who is wanted by the Dearborn county authorities on a grand larceny charge and who, it is believed, can clear up the heretofore impenetrable mystery surrounding the murder of pretty Rosa Kaiser, which occurred near Manchester station last May. At the time of the murder Pool was employed on the Big Four Railway improvements in progress between Manchester station and Guilford, Ind., and on the day preceding the crime he, in company with three suspicious-looking characters, were seen hanging about the Kaiser home. However, suspicion did not point to him until recently, when the police learned certain facts, which they do not care to disclose at present.

Sheriff Axby claims to have in his possession evidence implicating Pool in the murder of Rosa Kaiser, and believes that if the young man is arrested he will be glad to secure leniency by divulging all he knows about the case.

Detective Crawford, of Cincinnati, holds a warrant for Pool's arrest on the grand larceny charg
The murder of Rosa Kaiser is the darkest crime that ever blackened the criminal annal of Dearborn county. Late one evening in May, when the girl, in company with her aged father, Martin Kaiser, was returning home on foot from Yorkville Catholic Church, where the father and daughter had been attending Ascension day services, she was murdered in cold blood and her body thrown into West Fork, a branch of Tanner's creek, where it was found horribly mutilated a few days later. Martin Kaiser was attacked and felled to the earth unconscious by a blow from a heavy club dealt from behind, a gaping gash was made in his throat and he was beaten brutally. The assailant then threw him into the creek, where he revived hours afterward and made his way home more dead than alive. Kaiser did not witness the assault on his daughter, as she was many yards ahead of him, running to escape a heavy storm that was approaching. From this fact it would appear that the man was struck down first and the girl, seeing the attack on him rushed to his rescue and met her death. Her umbrella, which was broken about five inches from the tip, indicated that she had made a fierce struggle in defense of either her father or herself. Martin Kaiser did not see the assailant. The blow which rendered him unconscious was struck from behind, and he could give no details other than that he heard a footfall behind him, received the blow and all was blank. Some deductions in the case which have never been made public were the result of a personal investigation of the crime on the part of Marshal Theodore Crusse.

"When Kaiser was struck he was facing the west," said Mr. Crusse to a Journal representative this morning. "He carried an umbrella raised to keep off the rain
the west, said Mr. Crusse to a Journal representative this morning. "He carried an umbrella raised to keep off the rain which had just begun to fall. The storm was coming from the east, and therefore the umbrella was slanted in that direction. The blow which felled Kaiser was received upon the left side of his face and was dealt from behind. Such a blow must necessarily have been delivered by a lefthanded man. When the police capture a lefthanded suspect, I will share their belief in his possible guilt."

Heretofore all efforts to locate the murderer have proved futile. Shortly after the discovery of the crime the country for many miles about Manchester station was scoured by armed posses searching for the guilty one. They were aided by blood-hounds, but even the keen-scented manhunting dogs were at fault. Now it is hoped that the mystery will be at last cleared up, and the girl's murder avenged. Martin Kaiser, who has fully recovered from the effects of the assault, is heartbroken over the loss of his wife who died recently from the effects of the shock of her daughter's horrible death.

Rhea and Thurman

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

WINCHESTER, VA., August 28.—Captain James M. Haymaker, one of the most prominent citizens of Winchester, a Confederate veteran, fireman and Councilman, was murderously assaulted shortly after 11 o'clock last night by two drunken negro brutes, Shack Johnson and Henry Thompson, while he was discharging his duty as a special policeman and watchman at Baker and Company's wholesale merchandise house. He was knocked down and beaten in the face with his own revolver, and kicked and cuffed in a vicious manner. His life was saved by Charles Brown, a colored man, who scared the negroes off. Captain Haymaker's condition is quite serious.

The negro Thompson escaped on a freight train, but was arrested and will be brought back. The police prevented an infuriated crowd of armed men from making an attempt to lynch Johnson. He was hurriedly taken to jail and placed in a strong steel cage.

Arguments were begun in the Circuit Court this afternoon before Judge Thomas W. Harrison for attorney's fees and allowance by attorneys in the celebrated suit for divorce filed by Mrs. Thurman against her husband, General Charles Thurman, of Clarke county. A large crowd was attracted to the court-room in the City Hall to hear the speeches of Judge W. F. Rhea, of Bristol, and Lewis Bumgardner, of Staunton, for Mrs. Thurman, and Messrs. A. and Conrad Kownslar, of Berryville, for the defendant. So far no trouble has occurred between Judge Rhea and General Thurman, who have exchanged newspaper interviews. General Thurman is not here, but his wife is.

At 10 o'clock to-night Judge Harrison signed a decree allowing the complainant $40 per month for support, pending a proper presentation of the case to the court; $250 court expenses and $400 attorneys' fees, to be paid upon certified vouchers, all of which is to come from General Thurman.

WOULD-BE LYNCHERS.
Yesterday a new turn was given the Haymaker assault case in Winchester on which Shack Johnson, an negro tough, narrowly escaped lynching, when a number of well-known white men were arrested on complaint of Mollie Smith, colored, charged with breaking into her house Monday night and firing off revolvers. It was learned Monday night that Johnson's accomplice, Harry Johnson, was in hiding in Winchester. The police endeavored to locate him and searching parties of young men were formed. A report was spread that the negro was at the Smith woman's house, and an attack was made on the place. Revolvers were fired, the door was broken down and the place thoroughly scarched, but Johnson had escaped. The crowd fired their revolvers in the house, and if Johnson had been found he would undoubtedly have been lynched on the spot. Last night the members of the crowd who were arrested were discharged in the Winchester Police Court.

A mob of 50 masked men went to the jail at Shawneetown, Ill., yesterday morning and demanded that Jailer Galloway turn over to them John Griffin, colored, who was under arrest for an attempted assault on Mrs. Joseph Hobbs, a white woman, near her own home. Griffin had been frightened away by the woman's screams and had been arrested a short while afterward. When the mob demanded that Jailer Galloway turn the negro over to them Galloway armed himself, and after reasoning with the men from the jail door, he warned them that any effort to force the jail would be at their own peril. The mob, in spite of the jailer's words, made several ineffectual attempts to break down the jail doors, finally dispersing about daylight. Many of the colored people are taking sides with Griffin, though some of them have, in fear of a race riot, left the town. No trouble has followed the visit of the mob to the jail yesterday morning, but preparations are making to take the negro to Carmi for safekeeping.

NARROWLY ESCAPED LYNCHING
NEGROES MAKE A BRUTAL ASSAULT ON A WATCHMAN.
One of the Men Arrested and is Saved by the Timely Arrival of the Police.
Capt. James M. Haymaker, city councilman, of Winchester, was the victim late Thursday night of a murderous assault by two negroes, in which one of his assailants escaped lynching only by the timely arrival of the police. Captain Havmaker is a night watchman for Baker & Co., wholesale grocers.

About 11 o'clock "Shack" Johnson and another negro, who is thought to be Harry Wiltshire, of Atlanta, Ga.. got into an altercation. Afterward the men were walking up the railroad track cursing loudly, when Captain Haymaker ordered them to desist. Johnson knocked the aged night watchman down, and kicked the prostrate man in the face until he was unconscious. People were attracted to the scene and scared the negroes off. Search for the negroes was then instituted and Johnson was found. He resisted arrest, and was beaten almost into insensibility by the infuriated crowd. Twice on the way to the station house the prisoner was stopped with the intention of lynching. and as he entered the police station a man pointed a revolver against his heart.

As he was about to pull the trigger the police snatched the weapon from him.

Johnson was finally landed in a cell. Late yesterday Wiltshire was arrested at Brunswick, Md., and sentenced to four months in the Maryland House of Correction for stealing a ride on a freight train. The Virginia authorities will endeavor to have him brought to Winchester for trial.

FRIGHTENS
NEGROES
Bomb Fired to Get Them Out
of Holdenville.
CAUSEDGREATEXCITEMENT
People Thought That Frisco Train Had Been Held Up.
Holdenville, I. T., Jan. 28.—A few days ago negro help was employed at some of the hotels in Holdenville and immediately a strong sentiment was manifested and expressed at once against the action of the hotel keepers, and later the negroes were ordered to leave town, which they failed to do. On Saturday night about 11 o'clock some miscreant, in order to frighten them away, threw a dynamite bomb against the small building in the rear of one of the hotels used for servants' quarters, which smashed in the windows, and gave the house a general shaking up and causing a stampede of the negroes, who no longer hesitated about leaving but took the first train out of town.

The explosion of the dynamite caused great excitement, which was augmented by the fact that on the same evening the Frisco express, mail and passenger train had passed through under the guard of a heavily armed posse, and it was reported that the railway people were fearing a hold-up. On hearing the explosion many of the citizens grabbed their revolvers and Winchesters and rushed out expecting to find the bank being looted by a gang of outlaws, but when they reached that financial institution they found their fears without foundation, for the building had not been attacked and of course the cash was still resting in the vaults.

It was the most painfully exciting moment ever experienced in Holdenville, but when it was all over every citizen congratulated himself upon the fact that the worst damage to the town, if any existed, was the loss of the negro help and a few broken window glasses.

Hotel and Habitation of Colored Demestics Is Dynamited.

Holdenville, I. T., Jan. 29.—The negro question has assumed an acute form here. There is an unwritten law in this town that no negroes shall live here. Despite the prevailing sentiment against them, the necessity for domestics and hotel help has lead to the employment of a limited number. There is a strong sentiment against any member of the colored race landing here with intent to reside, and dire threats have been made against the negroes and those who employ them. This sentiment found violent expression in an outbreak last Saturday night when the habitation of the Hotel Scott and one or two of the domestics were dynamited. The explosion was terrific, rocking many buildings in the business section of the town and breaking the glass of many windows. The colored contingent, terrified, left town on the first outgoing train. In the meantime the problem of domestic help is still more complicated.

A party of colored girls, domestics, was accosted on the streets Sunday, and the man accused of the act was arrested and tried in the commissioner's court Tuesday on a charge of using vile and indecent language. The prosecution was backed by a number of the leading men of the town, who have decided to defend their domestic help despite the violent opposition of the community. The feeling is most bitter, and threatens to disrupt the harmony that has heretofore prevailed. It is not a question of race, but a question of competent domestic help that is the basis of the trouble.

Negro Shot on the Monticello Road.
A negro named Jesse Bagents was shot near the four-mile post on the Monticello road early Saturday night by unknown persons and left for dead. A younger brother of Jesse Bagents, who was with him at the time and escaped unhurt, came to town about 9 o'clock and reported the shooting to S. F. Magee and others, stating that his brother had been killed, and on Sunday morning Coroner Lambright empaneled a jury and went out to the scene of the shooting to hold an inquest on the body. On reaching the neighborhood the coroner learned that the negro was still alive, and after diligent inquiry and a trip for some distance through the wood, located him in a cabin in the neighborhood. It was discovered that he had been shot from the rear and freely peppered between the shoulders with No. 4 shot, but was likely to recover.

On being questioned Bagents stated that he and his brother were passing along the road together about dark when they passed three men standing on the road side whom they saluted politely and then passed on. When they had proceeded but a few steps, they were fired upon twice with a shot gun by the men they had passed and he fell to the ground and cried out that he was shot, and his brother ran to the bushes and escaped. The younger Bagents made substantially the same statement. They said the men who did the shooting were white men, but claimed they did not recognize any of them.

After the white men had disappeared and his brother had run off, the wounded man said he got up and made his way to the home of a sister of his who lived in the neighborhood, and on Sunday morning had gone in a buggy to the cabin where the jury of inquest found him.

Upon inquiry The Leader learns that Jesse Bagents is an insolent and overbearing negro and bears a bad reputation among his white neighbors. Justice Hoffman states that he was arraigned before him early in the year for using profane and abusive language to Pink Jordan, a white citizen of the county, and when the affidavit was read to him in court, reciting a part of the offensive language he had used to Mr. Jordan in the presence of his wife nd children, he promptly plead guilty and appeared proud and boastful of the insolence he had displayed on that occasion.

Such negroes as these will always excite the resentment and ill-will of their white neighbors, and should be taught the lesson they deserve, but shooting them in the back in the dark is not the right or manly way to do it.

Chattanooga, Tenn., July 24.—The details of the revolt of the convicts in the mines of the Georgia Iron and Coal Company at Cole City, Ga., were learned here tonight.

The revolt occurred this afternoon when the hour had arrived for the changing of the day and night shifts. So far only two convicts have been shot and they are probably fatally wounded, but about 125 other convicts of the day shift have barricaded themselves in the mines and refuse to come out and are defying the officers with their tools, threatening death to any one who approaches them.

The Dade Coal Mines are located about fifty miles from Chattanooga and are worked by Georgia convicts. The total force of convicts there about 200, 125 of whom work in the day time and the rest at night. Among the convicts are a number of men sentenced to life imprisonment and several desperate characters, the most of the convicts being negroes.

AT LAST ACCOUNTS THERE WAS NO CHANGE IN SITUATION AT GEORGIA CAMP—PROPERTY IS BARRICADED.
Atlanta, July 25.—No additional information has been received this morning at the office of the state prison commission regarding the mutiny of the 125 convicts of the Dade coal mines at Coal City, Ga., fifty miles south of Chattanooga, last night, in which it was reported that two of the convicts had been shot. The names of the convicts, who are known entirely by their numbers, have not yet been learned, but it is known that the men were ringleaders of the band who had barricaded themselves in the shaft of the mine.

It is said that the guards were forced to fire on the men on account of the menacing and threatening attitude of the convicts. It is learned that the shooting of the two prisoners may result fatally.

It is possible that the convicts had planned such a mutiny, and may have secreted food in the mines, and can withstand a siege for some time.

As the only way of escaping is through the mouth of the mine, the prisoners are powerless without arms, and it may be that the men may have to be forced to surrender by starvation.

The coal company has a strong barricade around their property, which is securely guarded, and there is hardly the barest chance for the men to overpower the guards unless supplied with weapons to make an attack.

The coal mines are the property of the Georgia Iron and Coal company. The representative of the company in this city had received no information in regard to the mutiny up to noon today further than the dispatches received by the prison commission last night.

MUTINY ENDS AT COLE CITY.
Beck and Jordan Were Shot Down Quelling the Disturbance. Because the number of guards at Cool
Because the number of guards at Coal City were considered insufficient, thirty-nine of the negro convicts who took part in Friday's mutiny were taken to the furnace at Rising Fawn, Ga.

With this departure and the strengthening of the guards now at Coal City, the situation at that place Sunday afternoon was one of quiet and order. In the morning Judge Turner, chairman of the state prison commission, and Deputy Warden Moore appeared before the convicts and made addresses in which they stated the authority of the guards, the provisions of the law and the fact that discipline must and would be maintained and if needs be at any cost.

The men who had been put in chains were then ordered to go back to work, and although there were some remonstrances, there were no open demonstrations of any kind and the convicts again resumed their regular duties. It is generally conceded that with the removal of the thirty-nine negroes the guards are sufficient to cope with any uprising and quell any movement at its very inception.

It now develops that the whole trouble started Friday morning because one Henry Lowe, who cursed a guard, refused to be whipped. When an effort was made in this direction he made a dash at Deputy Warden Goode with a heavy piece of timber and threatened to brain the officer. Immediately 125 other convicts joined in the mutiny and rushed upon the officers.

With the first intimation of the assault five guards fired and as a result Joe Beck, a long term convict from south Georgia, had his cheek shot off with buckshot. "Snaps" Jordan, also from south Georgia, was shot through the leg, and another negro had his shirt front shot away and was wounded in the breast. All of the three negroes shot were leaders in the uprising.

Lowe and another negro were whipped after the trouble was settled and the convicts were placed on a diet of bread and water and threatened with no sustenance. These vigorous measures had the effect of quelling the mutiny very soon and the men seemed glad to go back to work on any terms of peace.

ATTEMPT TO LYNCH A NEGRO.
Philadelphia Firemen Rescue Him From Mob Just in Time.
The Philadelphia Press of today says: An enraged crowd of nearly three hundred persons held up and surrounded a trolley car in front of the Passyunk square at 13th and Wharton streets last night, in an effort to capture and lynch a negro who, it is said, had assaulted a white man a few blocks away.

It was only through the remarkable bravery displayed by the crew of fire truck No. 11, which has its headquarters on 12th street below Wharton, that the negro was saved from the fury of the mob. The firemen leaving a lone man to guard the "joker" in case of an alarm, ran in a body across the open square in front of their house, and by sheer force fought their way to the heart of the mob. Then after they had closed in on the negro they fought their way back again and succeeded in reaching the fire station and closing the door just in time to prevent the place being taken by storm.

All this while the policemen on that beat were elsewhere and the first notification of trouble to reach the Snyder avenue station came when the fire crew sent in a call for help. The arrival of a patrol wagon filled with policemen alone caused the mob to break up and scatter through the square and nearby streets and alleys.

John Thompson, the negro whose life for nearly an hour was in the hands of the mob, it is said, knocked down and beat a white man at 13th and Ellsworth streets, just a block north of the square. As he ran, a crowd followed shouting at his heels. The chase led by the square in which hundreds were seated on the benches and to the cries of the first body of pursuers were soon added the wild clamor of the additional throng.

When the negro reached Dickinson street he sought to elude his pursuers by leaping on a car bound north in 13th street. The leaders in the pursuit called back for the others to head off the car and by the time it reached Reed street at the southern terminus of the square a dense mob had ranged itself across the street, forming a barrier to the car's further progress.

A dozen men leaped on the front platform and in a jiffy the motorman's arms were pinned and the power was shut off. The conductor was likewise besieged on the rear end of the car and at the same time dozens in the crowd attempted to climb through the window.

All this time the negro, scared almost to death, crouched low in the car, behind two women passengers. He had about given up hope, when the firemen from the truck house made their way in a body to the steps of the car. Armed with whatever they could pick up before leaving the house, these men faced the mob and succeeded in breaking through in time to rescue the negro from a dozen men who already had hold of him. Then back through the car, the mob and across the square they fought until the fire station was again reached.

The other attempt to lynch a negro was in Philadelphia, where a bad negro, who had made an unprovoked assault upon a white man. It took a whole fire company to rescue the negro from the mob, composed of 500 men, who were crying out: "Lynch him," "Hang him," and trying to carry out their admonition. It should teach Pennsylvanians not to lecture Southern men who show the same spirit. It is wrong, whether displayed in the North or the South. There has been some general talk to-day about appealing to President Roosevelt for Regular army troops should rioting on an extensive scale break out or seem imminent. There are only about twelve hundred National Guardsmen in Delaware, and nearly half of these are in Wilmington.

An incipient riot broke out on Ninth street between Walnut and King at a late hour this evening, which, had it occurred earlier, when the crowds were still thick on the streets, might have been sufficient to have put the city in an uproar. The negroes in arming themselves to-day did so, as they said, to resist any such attacks upon them as were made repeatedly last evening while the mob was in possession of the streets.

Later this evening the armed negroes became more aggressive in their demeanor. They began marching about in bands of considerable force, ostentatiously carrying clubs and other weapons besides those concealed on their persons.

A gang of this kind, a hundred or more in number, were assembled in Ninth street between Walnut and King. A party of white men came along and there was a collision. Which began it nobody quite knows. The negroes opened a fusillade of pistol shots which hit nobody, but brought down upon them a squad of some twenty policemen under Sergt. McDermott.

The sergeant started to arrest a negro named Leander Moon, who fired at him, the ball grazing the officer's cheek. At the same moment Joseph S. Shockley, another negro, fired at McDermott and hit Policeman Evans, making a wound that was a mere scratch.

While all this was going on whites and negroes were emptying their revolvers as fast as possible. So far as can be learned, although about two hundred shots were fired only one person, save the two policemen wounded, was hit.

This was a negro, who was struck by a stray bullet, which inflicted a slight wound. The police did not fire a shot, but they gave Moon and Shockley a sound clubbing and brought them as prisoners to the police station.

The negro mob was then surrounded and held in check by the police, while other policemen, at a distance, prevented white men from entering the block where the disturbance occurred. This prompt action and the lateness of the hour prevented serious consequences.

The mob element had pretty much disappeared from the streets and the news is not likely to reach them in time to stir them up.
