(Special to The Evening World.)

WILMINGTON, Del., June 26.—William Simms, colored, of Tarrytown, N. Y., has confessed he shot William Kramer, colored, who died in the Delaware Hospital early to-day.

Shortly before midnight about twenty-five negroes congregated opposite the French street station. When Kramer used an insulting remark toward Simms the latter shot him in the abdomen.

Sergts. Kelleher and Bagley found Simms two hours later hiding in an alley way. Simms was held without bail.

One white man and two negroes were sentenced to the Workhouse this morning by Judge Cochran, in the City Court, for acts of lawlessness during the past two days.

At Ninth and King streets, last night, there was general disorder for a time, caused by a white man having been assaulted by colored men. Shortly afterward Sergt. McDermott and squad heard many shots fired and went to the scene. As the police reached the place of disorder Leander Moore fired point blank at Sergt. McDermott. The bullets entered his right eyebrow. Sergt McDermott grabbed Moore and got a blow from his revolver that cut the Sergeant's forehead.

Patrolman Simmons grabbed a negro named Shockley. A bullet struck him on his shoulder, but did no injury.

Moore pleaded guilty to assault and battery and Judge Cochran sentenced him to one year.

Shockley pleaded guilty to the charge of disorderly conduct, and the Court sentenced him to pay a fine of $50 and costs. He will go to the Workhouse this afternoon.

City Solicitor Reinhart, in asking for a heavy sentence in the case of John Joyce, a young white man who assaulted a colored woman, said that such an act might have been the spark to send off a powder magazine. Joyce was sent up for six months.

Friends of Gov. Hunn said to-day that it is probable that the militia will be called out unless there is a speedy subsidence of the mob spirit, which is still in evidence. Many of the citizens will appeal to the Governor for troops.

Magistrate Holls at noon dismissed the charge of murder preferred against Arthur Corwell, who was arrested in connection with the cremation of the negro. An alibi was proven.

Judge George Gray, of the United States Court, says he approves the statement given by ex-Congressman Handy that the lynching of White cannot be approved and there is great reason to regret that it occurred.

"But judicious men," he adds, "cannot forget the provocation which stirred our people to their desperate action. Like provocation would probably be followed by a similar explosion in any country inhabited by our race anywhere in the world."

"The part of wisdom is to let the matter pass quietly into history, without any additional excitement and without anything else to regret. The denunciation of the people has already been full enough and harsh enough. Let it cease. It would, I think, be the part of wisdom for the Attorney-General's office to treat the matter as a closed incident, for the reason, if no other, that attempted prosecutions would probably put a strain on the jury system which it would not sustain and convictions would not be obtained on any evidence."

CORWELL TO HAVE HEARING
INDIANA MAN WHO IS CHARGED WITH BEING A LYNCHER.
Charge of Murder to Be Changed to Manslaughter—Governor Hunn Denounces the Mob.
WILMINGTON, Del., June 25.—A riot broke out in the streets late to-night between whites and negroes and for a time assumed serious proportions. The arrival of a squad of police, however, quickly dispersed the participants. Two arrests were made. A large gang of negroes, which had been marching up and down Ninth street, was challenged by about twenty-five white men, and in the fight that followed a hundred shots were exchanged.

A squad of policemen under Captain Evans and Sergeant McDermott charged the mob. The negroes and whites fled, but the police captured two negroes, Leander Moore and Joseph Shockley. The policemen used their clubs freely and in the melee attendant on the arrests McDermott and Patrolman Green received slight wounds. One negro, James Mercer, was shot in the head during the riot, but his wound is not believed to be serious.

In a brawl in another part of the city William Cramer, a negro, was shot in the stomach by a white man. He was taken to a hospital in a serious condition.

The leaders of the party of negroes who were marching in Ninth street to-night declared that they intended to resent the attacks made on members of their race last night. They say they have been abused and that they do not intend to quietly submit to such abuse. They say they have no sympathy for George F. White, the negro who was lynched for murdering Miss Helen Bishop.

Arthur Corwell, of Indiana, who was arrested in connection with the lynching, will be given a hearing to-morrow. It was the intention of the police to give him a hearing this afternoon but for some reason it was postponed. At the hearing tomorrow the charge of murder will be changed to that of manslaughter. Corwell's bond of $5,000 was renewed, Thomas McHugh, a wholesale liquor dealer, and Col. James P. McComb, a capitalist of Claymont, going bail.

In an interview to-day, Governor Hunn said: "Conditions at Wilmington are a great humiliation to the entire State. I have come here against my physician's orders to get a grasp on the situation. The way things have progressed is most serious; what has been done so far by mobs I do not think could have been prevented by the authorities, but a halt must be called instantly. After hearing of the mob's work last night in forcing the release of the prisoner, I felt that I could not stand back any longer. The fair name of Delaware has been dragged in the mire. It was no ordinary mob that released the man who murdered Miss Bishop. The crowd seems to have been composed of good citizens. The effect of their work has been disastrous. The law must now be sustained at any cost, I have not yet decided whether or not troops will be called out. I trust that will not be necessary, but the whole power of the State will be used to protect its officers in the discharge of their duties."

WILMINGTON, Del., June 26.—Col. Wickersham and Major Doherty of the First Regiment, Delaware National Guard, with a squad of men took possession of the State armory in this city to-night. Their object was to prevent a possible raid upon the armory.

A Gatling gun was stationed at the entrance and the work of burnishing arms and getting them in readiness for possible use went on until a late hour. The guard will be continued all night. Col. Wickersham said he had received no instructions from the Governor, but as custodian of the armory and its contents he deemed it best to be prepared.

The request of the Mayor that children be kept from the streets was well observed to-night. The fact that no crowd was permitted to gather had an excellent effect, and it is believed that the worst is over. There are, however, vague rumors of what may be done to-morrow night. There is a half holiday on Saturday, and the danger will be increased when the usual Saturday crowds gather. It is possible that the saloons will be closed until Monday.

Judge George Gray of the Third United States Circuit Court, it was said this afternoon, had offered to go bail for Arthur Corwell in the event of his being held for trial. When questioned on the subject he said:

"It is an occasion when the least said the better. I think it a most regrettable and deplorable occurrence, and the sooner order is restored the better it will be. I hope that our citizens will be quiet and refrain from exciting talk and anything that will continue the excitement of the past few days.

"I thoroughly indorse the views expressed by Mr. Hardy. I did not offer to furnish bail for Corwell, but if he had been held in bail I would have been as willing as other citizens would to go on his bond. That is only one of the orderly processes of the law and has no significance."

As a result of last night's riots, William Kramer, a negro, who was shot in a fracas on what is known as "the coast," a negro district, died at the Delaware Hospital at 3 o'clock this morning.

Several negroes in different parts of the city were shot, and what began as a clash between white and black men reached its climax in a fight among negroes themselves. This occurred about midnight, 100 yards from the Pennsylvania railroad station, and it was during this trouble that Kramer was shot.

William Simms, a negro, with whom Kramer had had an argument, was arrested by the police and in the City Court this morning was charged with murder and held without bail to await the action of the Coroner's jury.

Two men who were arrested during last night's rioting, Leander Moore and Joseph Shockley, both negroes, were also arraigned in the City Court this morning before Judge Cochran. Moore was charged with striking Police Sergeant McDermott on the head with the butt of a revolver. He was convicted and sentenced to one year in the county workhouse.

Shockley was accused of shooting a revolver, although he was not seen to point the weapon at anybody. He was sentenced to pay a fine of $50 and the costs of the prosecution, which will mean imprisonment if he is unable to pay.

Arthur Corwell, the only man arrested for participation in the burning of the negro White, was acquitted and released to-day after a hearing.

The hearing took place at the office of Magistrate Hollis. Corwell, who was present with his bondsman, was represented by former Congressman L. Irving Handy and former Deputy City Judge Sylvester D. Townsend, Jr. Attorney-General H. H. Ward and his deputy, Robert H. Richards looked after the interests of the State. The court room was filled to suffocation and the crowd blocked the street outside.

Detective Francis, who was the first witness, testified that he arrested Corwell as a result of a conversation between Corwell and a man of the name of Saunders as to what they saw at the burning of White, and swore that Saunders had said that Corwell was one of the men brought here to do the job. He did not see Corwell at the prison or at the burning.

Chief of Police George Black testified that he saw Corwell in the corridor of the workhouse. Warden A. S. Meserve of the workhouse identified Corwell as having been present in the attack on the workhouse. He saw him in the third vestibule of the west wing and heard him give directions to the workers.

THREE MEN WOUNDED

WILMINGTON, JUNE 23th.—While quelling an outbreak of turbulent negroes tonight two policemen were slightly wounded and a negro was shot.

For awhile the row threatened to assume the proportions of a race riot, as white men in the vicinity went to the aid of the policemen, but was finally restored after many shots had been fired and two negroes were arrested. The trouble was fomented by a dispute over the recent lynching.

Sergeant Engena McDermott and Patrolman Francis Green were the policemen injured, but their injuries are very slight wounds about the face, while James A. Marcér, colored, of 400 East Twelfth street, who was in the throng, received a scalp wound, evidently from a revolver bullet.

Negroes Carried Clubs

Two hundred negroes carrying clubs congregated in the vicinity of Ninth and Walnut Streets about 8 o'clock and marched along Ninth Street, knocking down a white man at King Street and a white boy in front of the post office, poking a revolver in his face.

Later the disorderly crowd returned to Ninth and Walnut Streets, and a squad of twenty policemen, commanded by Captain Evans, was sent to disperse them. They talked of getting revenge for the rough treatment of negroes by the mob last night, but no trouble occurred there.

Attracted by the unusual gathering of negroes, many white men congregated in the vicinity out of curiosity, and one of them, named Chamberlain, at Ninth and King streets, was slapped in the face by a negro, after which the negroes began to shoot revolvers, crying, "Let's clean the corner."

Whites Retaliated

Some of the white men retaliated with revolvers until Sergeant McDermott and a few policemen arrived. McDermott saw Leader Moore, colored, with a revolver in his hand and started for him. Moore fired point blank at McDermott, but the bullet passed over his shoulder and struck Patrolman Green on the cheek. McDermott grappled with Moore, who pounded the officer with the butt of a revolver until he was clubbed into submission.

Street Blocked Off

A spent bullet struck MrDermott on the forehead. Patrolman Green, although wounded, seized Joseph S. Shockley, another negro flourishing a revolver, and Moore and Shockley were taken to the police station charged with inciting to riot.

After the arrests the policemen blocked off the street and refused to allow any persons to traverse it and also dispersed the main body of negroes congregated two blocks away. No further disorder is anticipated. The entire police force is patrolling the streets, giving the order "Keep moving" to loiterers.

Adjutant I. Pusey Wickersham was at the Armory, but no militiamen were present.

May Call Out Militia

It was reported shortly before midnight that Adjutant - General Wickersham would call out the State militia in the morning, but this was not done.

An autopsy was held on the body of Peter Smith, the Italian bey, to-night, and a 44-calibre bullet was found in his abdomen. This strengthens the theory that he was shot by a guard at the workhouse.
Thought Incident Was Closed

Up to the hour of this sudden outbreak matters had begun to resume their normal condition, and it was generally believed that the State had seen the end of the era af excitement and mob rule that has been in evidence in New Castle County since Helen Bishop met her death and her murderer, the negro, George White, paid the penalty by being burned at the stake at the hands of thousands of citizens.

Governor Conferes With Law Officers

Governor Hunn arrived in this city this morning, and there was no secret that his purpose here was to confer with others regarding the riotous conditions that have prevailed in the county during the week. In the conference, together with the Governor, were Chief Justice Lore, Associate Judges Grubb, Spruence and Penniwell, Attorney General Ward, Deputy Attorney General Richards, City Solicitor Reinhardt, Mayor Fisher and Police Commissioners Stayton, Clarkson and Jones.

The conference was in session for more than two hours, and at its conclusion none of those present would discuss what took place. If was declared that it was purely of a private nature.

Notwithstanding this, it was learned on good authority that the whole purport of the conference was to decide upon a line of action that would prevent a repetition of the scenes of last night.

After weighing matters, it was said, the Governor and the others in the conference came to the conclusion that the only course to pursue in the face of the public feeling was to make no more arrests until such time as public feeling had subsided.

DELAWARE SCENE OF TROUBLE
Shots Exchanged in Wilmington and Several are Seriously Hurt More Trouble Expected

Wilmington, Del., July 1.—A riot broke out in the streets here late last night between whites and negroes but the arrival of the police quickly dispersed the participants. Two negroes were arrested. A gang of negroes numbering probably 200, which had been marching up and down Ninth street, were challenged by about 25 white men and in the battle that followed over 100 shots were exchanged. Policeman McDermott and Green received slight wounds. One negro, James Mercer, was shot in the head but his wound was not believed to be serious. In a brawl in another part of the city, a negro was shot in the stomach by a white man. He was taken to the hospital in a serious condition.

The leaders of the negroes who were marching on Ninth street, declared they intended to resent the attacks made upon members of their race the night before. They say they have no sympathy for White, the negro lynched here, but that most of the negroes in and about Wilmington approve of it.

Leander Moore and Joseph Shockley, negroes, arrested for shooting Policemen McDermott and Green during the disturbance last night, were adjudged guilty of inciting a riot. Portion of Eastern Section Buried in Water.
TEN THOUSAND HOMELESS
Midnight Riot Guns Call Slumbering Residents From Beds to Face the Flood.
ST. LOUIS, June 10.—One-half of East St. Louis is buried in the flood. Ten thousand persons are homeless, and at the mercy of the raging waters.

Families are prisoners in the garrets of their homes, or on their roofs. They are without food, and are crying for help. Two thousand people who sought refuge in the Washington Hotel, the Franklin School, St. Mary's Church, and the plant of the St. Louis Syrup Refining Company, are prisoners, and are suffering greatly.

Dike Broke After Midnight.

The break in the Illinois Central dike came at thirty minutes after midnight. In five minutes a mighty torrent was tearing through the large residence section in the eastern part of the city. The people, thousands of whom were in bed, felt certain that the city was safe, but were warned by the blowing of the sand train whistles, by the firing of riot guns, and the cries of those who had been working on the embankment in an effort to save it.

The property losses cannot be estimated. Many industries are flooded. Many are not only made homeless, losing all of their worldly possessions, but are thrown into idleness. This city is in dire need.

Thirty Feet of Water.

The water stands from three to thirty feet deep all over the eastern half of the city. Houses are weakening and falling. The destruction seems complete. The flood came down upon the city from the back water in the southeast. At 8 o'clock this morning the flood had swept clear through to the river and the city lies under in unbroken stretch of rising, swirling torrents.

It is conservatively estimated that thirty persons were drowned last night in East St. Louis. Other estimates are as high as 100.

One hundred men who were working on the dike at the time of the break narrowly escaped. Many were caught in the flood shoulder deep. Many swam to safety. It is feared that several were lost. The dike had been considered safe and all labor had been concentrated on the western and northern dikes.

Water Cut Passage.

Shortly after midnight the water cut a small passage through the embankment. Within two minutes this break had spread for a distance of forty feet, with a torrent crashing through. The workers saw that there was no hope and the sand trains backed down into the city, their whistles blowing shrill blasts of warning. The guards who had patrolled the dike fired their riot guns in all directions and ran down through the streets shouting their warning to the sleeping citizens.

The workers fled for their lives. The women and children who had been at work on the dikes for six hours filling the sacks with which the embankment was strengthened, ran in panic.

Chief of Police Purdy, of East St Louis, at 5 o'clock this morning sent an urgent appeal to the St. Louis authorities. He said 10,000 lives were in peril. Boats or anything that will float are urgently asked for. Steps were taken to lend all aid in the power of St. Louisans.

St. Louis, June 10.—Almost two-thirds of the territory embraced by East St. Louis is under from two to fifteen feet of water. Between twilight last night and dawn today eleven lives were sacrificed to the angry waters and damage which no man today attempts to estimate has been done to property. Not a wheel of industry is turning in East St. Louis, but the flood waters whirl and suck at the foundations of many great buildings that have been deserted and the vast railroad yards can only be located by hundreds of half submerged cars and locomotives. Huge grain elevators stand surrounded by running water. To the south beyond the railway yards are thousands of cottages owned by laborers and containing their all, submerged to the eaves.

In northern East St. Louis the condi-toin is not so bad.

The business portion of the city and the district containing the better residences is still intact, but for how long is not known. Broadway, running from Eads bridge east to the city limits, a wide street built of sand and walled with stone, fifteen feet high, divides the city in halves. Over ten feet of water is pressing against Broadway from the south and in many places is seeping through in streams as thick as a man's body. Traffic over certain portions of the thoroughfare has been prohibited.

If Broadway breaks the water will rush over much of the city until Missouri avenue, parallel one block north, is encountered. Along the river front to the west a levee of sand bags two to six feet high and two miles long keeps the river.

Last night the river suddenly began to rise. Tired men worked with energy to strengthen the sand bag levee. The city was safe all along the river front, but word was received that the Illinois Central embankment, skirting the river along the southern boundary of the city, was about to give way. Couriers were sent to shout warnings to the inhabitants of the southern half of the city and hundreds of laborers and citizens hastened to strengthen the embankment. Locomotives rushed car loads of sand bags to the place and work was hurriedly begun. Accustomed by this time to warnings of impending danger, the inhabitants did not leave their homes. Higher and higher crept the water until a thin stream began to pour over the embankment and suddenly it broke.

The break occurred at 11:40 o'clock. D. H. Sherwood, a laborer, was swept away and drowned. A section of the embankment was torn out and a stream twenty-five feet wide rushed through. It is believed that many men, especially negroes, were drowned.

The alarm spread like wildfire and whistles were blown, bells rung, shots fired and cries of warning were counded, but even with all this pandemonium, many of the inhabitants failed to leave their homes. Within an hour the streets stood in water that reached to the roofs of one-story cottages. Many fled to the brick buildings. NEW ORLEANS, Nov. 14.—The lynching at Pass Christian, Miss., of the negro, Sam Adams, for an assault on Mrs. Peter Labouisse, was accompanied by some features new in mob outbreaks of the kind. The novel features have received great popular approval in Mississippi and the affair has been pronounced the ideal of what a lynching should be, if lynch law is to be resorted to as a means of punishing assaults on women.

The Coroner's jury in the case declared that crimes of the kind should be punished by sudden and violent death. Heretofore juries have usually dodged the issue, but the Pass Christian jury was outspoken, and laid down a doctrine which is accepted in most parts of the South.

As for the lynching, it was the quietest and least disorderly ever known in Mississippi. Adams was executed by a committee instead of by the officers of the law, after a trial before a committee of citizens instead of a trial by court, and without the horrors that have so often accompanied Southern lynchings. The negroes of the town and county were not only not interfered with, but were actually asked to join the whites in the summary action thought necessary as a warning and a preventive of other similar crimes.

Pass Christian is probably the most conservative town in Mississippi, and unquestionably has the largest number of Northern residents. VALPARAISO, Ind., Aug. 8.—For a time to-night it was feared an attempt would be made to lynch a negro who is in jail here under guard. The determined stand taken by the sheriff, however, cooled the ardor of the would-be lynchers, and at midnight all was quiet on the streets.

About 4 o'clock this afternoon, while Mrs. U. S. Biggs, a young woman thirty years of age, who is the wife of a Washington township, Porter county, farmer, was alone at her home with two small children, a negro, who afterwards gave his name to the authorities as John Wilson, and a stranger, came to the door and asked for matches to go to a field to roast some corn. He later returned and asked for salt and pepper. While on this trip Wilson caught Mrs. Biggs by the throat and choked and kicked her while attempting to criminally assault her. Mrs. Biggs is now in a very critical condition.

When the crime became known relatives and farmers in the vicinity, armed with shotguns, formed a posse of nearly 100, which started in pursuit of the negro.

At Winslow Station, the nearest village, the telephone was used to notify officers in surrounding towns of the crime. The negro escaped the posse, jumped on a freight train and went to Wanatah, ten miles west of Valparaiso. Here Deputy Sheriffs Matthews and Billy Wilson, the latter a school teacherj and pugilist, saw the negro and ordered him to stop. The negro drew a long knife and threatened to kill them. Wilson picked up a stone, struck the negro and felled him to the ground.

Matthews and Wilson brought the negro to the county jail here while Sheriff Lacount and a score of deputies were searching the roads. The prisoner arrived at the jail here at 8:30 to-night and gave his name as John Wilson, saying he was from Pittsburg, Pa., and that he had been working on the railroad. At the jail Wilson was surly and declined to talk of the affair, although asking queer questions. The officers believe he is feigning insanity. Farmers living in the vicinity of the Biggs home and people here are greatly incensed and neighbors and Biggs's friends threaten violence.

Sheriff Lacount said to-night: "I do not fear an outbreak of a mob, but if there is I have a dozen armed men here in case of mob violence."

White Men Warn a Colored Man to Leave His Home.
NO NEGROES WANTED
Officials Present but Not in Force to Act.
Oklahoma City, O. T., Aug. 1.—At about 1 o'clock Friday morning an episode occurred in Orchard park which indicates that the breaking out of race troubles in other parts of the country, may be expected at any time in this city, says the Oklahoma.

Wibur Shepard, an employee at the Delmar Garden theatre was returning to his home after the performance late Wednesday night. He saw a number of armed men out by the woolen mill on West Main street, and not being able to distinguish them clearly in the darkness, concluded they were strange tramps and was mue alarmed over the discovery, as himself and wife reside in an isolated locality in the western suburbs of the city.

His wife being with him Shepard returned to the store at the corner of Main street and Western avenue and telephoned to Deputy Sheriff at Delmar Garden.

The deputy summoned a policeman at the park and, accompanied by two other men proceeded to the locality where the armed men had been seen.

In a short while they located a party of men in the front of a small frame house and were engaged in an angry conversation with its occupant, who proved to be a negro.

From the drift of the conversation it was discovered that the midnight visitors were ordering the negroes to remove from the neighborhood and threatening rough usage in case the warning should not be heeded. They gave the negroes twenty-four hours in which to remove with their belongings from Orchard park, which, they declared, was a white man's residence district and should remain so at any cost.

The officers approached the party and endeavored to throw a flash light upon the leaders of the party, but immediately found themselves looking into the frowning muzzles of a dozen winchesters and received the order to "git," which command they lost no time in obeying, regarding it as foolhardy to attempt to arrest any of the men in the party who were all seen to be masked and thoroughly armed.

The officers differ in their estimate of the number of men in the party, the policeman declaring his belief there were twenty-five, while deputy sheriff thought there were forty. The west end resident who first saw the armed party says there were about a dozen men in all.

The matter was presented to the city and county authorities and a deputy sheriff and a policeman were detailed to visit the scene again last night. In case a party was assembled to molest the negro resident the officers were instructed to command the peace and if necessary request the marauders to submit to arrest, but were warned not to imperil their lives unnecessarily.

The officers visited the locality at about eleven o'clock last night, but there were no signs of a recurrence of the visit by the mob. It is not believed by the authorities that the incident is closed, however, as the spokesman of the mob in his warning to the negroes the night previous, said; "We may not return tomorrow night, nor the next night, nor the next night, nor the night following, but we will return again soon and if you do not pack up and get out of here you will regret it."

The officers who encountered the party of armed and masked men on Wednesday night or Thursday morning, as it occurred after midnight, say they seemed terribly in earnest and do not doubt that there is trouble ahead. The authorities, however, are disposed to prevent any violence and will undoubtedly dispatch a posse of deputies and squad of police men to the locality at the first intimation of trouble.

It is said that there are two negro families residing in the house which was visited and they did not move out yesterday nor manifest any inclination to do so.

Constitution Bureau, 467 Second Street, Macon, Ga., June 24.—(Special.)—Shy, Glawson and Turner, the three young men who were arrested one day last week charged with holding a negro named Waters in a "condition of slavery," were arraigned before Judge Speer in the United States court this morning and to the charge entered a plea of guilty.

The cases have attracted no little attention here, and the court room was crowded when the defendants were called upon to answer the charge lodged against them. There was nothing dramatic in the scene. It was a plain everyday case in court, and when the defendants admitted their guilt no one was in the least surprised. With the plea of guilty submitted, what promised to be one of the most sensational cases known in this judicial circuit was all over except the sentence of Judge Speer. Judge Speer lost no time in bringing these peonage cases to a conclusion. His sentence was brief and impressive and during its delivery the crowd gave him an undivided attention. In passing sentence, Judge Speer said:

"You have been indicted for a crime in the execution of which you have held a citizen of the United States in a state of involuntary servitude, in other words, for a time you have held a citizen in a condition of slavery. This you have done by force and violence.

"The offense not only in its nature, but in its penalty as defined by law, is one of very serious consequence. The maximum penalty is imprisonment at hard labor in the penitentiary for five years or a fine of $5,000, or both. This is its first instance so far as I know in the state of Georgia. While this is true, and while the wrong you have done this colored man is palpable, it is also true you had no conception that you were violating the laws of the United States. I make allowance for this fact.

"You seem to be respectable men, fairly representative of that line class who constitute the farmers of Georgia. You are young men and, no doubt, passionate and had some feeling of exasperation toward the person of color who had obtained an advance upon his contract, and who quit his work in such manner as to inflict loss upon one of your number. This, however, did not justify you in violently seizing him and in attempting by force and threats to compel him in unwilling servitude to work out the amount of his indebtedness. The problems of this people are serious enough at best and they will be fearfully intensified if
threats to compel him in unwilling servitude to work out the amount of his indebtedness. The problems of this people are serious enough at best and they will be fearfully intensified if there is an attempt to solve them by the bullet or the lash. The laws forbid such inhumanity, the awakened conscience of the public will not tolerate, nor the criminal courts condone it. Imprisonment for debt is a violation of the organic law of our own state. Involuntary servitude as a punishment for crime, except after conviction by due process of law, is denounced by the constitution of the United States and the statute under which you are indicted.

He was soon traced there, and Sly and Turner brought him back tied to the back axle of the buggy, whipping him cruelly all the way.

The negro's wife managed to get to Macon, where she swore out the warrants securing the arrest of his assailants.

It is fair to the better class in the Southern States that these abuses are not practiced or permitted on most of the plantations. The labor contracts, according to the law, must be executed in the presence of a Magistrate, who explains to the laborers the terms, which must be as the Magistrate approves of. On most of the large plantations, which are conducted in a humane, business-like manner, the negroes are held to a careful execution of their contracts. They are worked a certain number of hours every day, and made to work all the time, and accounts are kept with them as to the supplies furnished, but the laws are such that harsh, unscrupulous and unjust men can take advantage of them to extort unpaid labor from the negroes, and practice the greatest cruelties upon them.

A great many offenses charged against the whites are directly in violation of the State laws, but there is nobody to take the poor negro's part, and the interpretation of the laws everywhere is likely to be such as some drunken brute of a white man may choose to give it.

The action of Judges Speer and Jones will rectify a large part of the most flagrant abuses. They pronounced features of the contract labor law as directly unconstitutional, and therefore void, and Judge Speer delivered a stirring lecture to the Federal Grand Jury, commanding it to throughly investigate the system of peonage in Georgia.

Trifling Offense the Basis. The negro is charged with some insignificant offense by the white man and is fined an enormous amount in comparison with the offense. A still better trick is to charge the negro with threats of violence and have him put under bond by the too friendly Magistrate. Then the white man, who has really provoked the entire prosecution, steps in and offers to go on the negro's bond or to pay his fine. The law in both Georgia and Alabama permits the defendant in such a case to hire himself out to the man who pays his fine or goes on his bond. The law expressly provides, however, that this contract must be made in open court, so that it can have the approval of the Magistrate. Under such a contract the man who pays the fine or assumes the bond can hold the laborer in his employ until the debt thus created and acknowledged in open court is satisfied. There are times when this proceeding is entirely humane and the negro gladly resorts to it to escape the terrors of a convict camp. It is obvious that even when such a
system is honestly administered and the scant safeguards the law has thrown about it are fully observed the ignorant negro, who can neither read nor write, who has no roof over his head, no food to put into his mouth, and no ballot to redress his wrongs, invariably gets the worst of it. But the poor white trash element are not satisfied with this large gambler's percentage, and so have gone outside of and beyond the law. Having secured the negro as a contract laborer, they have interpreted the law to mean that every subsequent advance in cash or goods to the negro is part of the original contract and must be worked out by involuntary servitude in the same way. Furthermore, a custom has grown up of making these contracts entirely outside of the court, where the negro has not even the protection of a white Magistrate.

Trumped up charges, collusion with unscrupulous Justices, combined with an unfair and unmanly trading upon the gross ignorance of the negro, have resulted in transferring many of the black men into actual and, as they believe, perfectly legal slavery, which they have chosen in preference to the admitted misery of a convict's life. Th's kind of peonage is chiefly built up on fraud, violence and misrepresentation.

Case That Started Inquiry.

What started Judge Speer to stir up the grand jury was the arrest ten days ago of three young men in Jasper county, Ga. — Will Shy, Arthur Glawson and Frank Turner. They were released on bail, and the facts in their case are now in possession of the District Attorney. The prosecution is Will Waters, a negro who alleges that he was held in actual slavery. He had made a contract to work for Shy from January until August, and, like all negroes, obtained one advance of money and rations after another. All of a sudden he found himself in debt for $35 beyond the full amount of his contract, and, thereupon, according to the usual negro custom, skipped out of the plantation during the night and went to work for another planter a dozen miles or so away. He was, of course, traced there, and Shy and Turner drove after him in a buggy, tied him to the back axle, and carried him back at full speed, the negro being dragged a part of the way and whipped incessantly both en route and on arrival at the old plantation. The negro's wife managed to get down to Macon, where she swore out the necessary warrants to secure his release and the arrest of his captors.

This particular case, which is almost identical with one minutely described to me by an educated young white planter many miles to the south of Jasper county, is not of the class referred to above, where peonage has been created by an unfair application of the criminal law and through fear of the convict stockade. On the contrary, these three young white men of Jasper county were acting under the well-known contract labor law of Georgia, which is practically identical with the statute of Alabama, just declared unconstitutional by Judge Jones in a luminous decision which has been widely printed and commented upon.

Under this contract labor law the planter makes written agreements with as many laborers as he may need. These contracts are generally signed immediately after the holidays and run, as a rule, until after the cotton is "set aside," which is the ordinary expression for the conclusion of the period of cultivation.

Throughout all the rural cotton counties of Georgia and Alabama, as well as of many other States, the system of contracts for labor is adopted by all the large white planters and by many of the negro planters as well. Here in Lee county, Ala., there is not so much of this vicious system, but it exists and can be easily traced. According to the census this county had in 1900 12,759 whites and 19,067 negroes. Of this latter class of black men and women there were reported to be no less than 7,483, or much more than one-third of the total, who were above ten years of age, and yet could neither read nor white. I know that the negro foreman on one plantation can neither read nor write, does not know how old he is, and cannot understand anything beyond the most babyish English.

NEWS OF THE DAY.
In an address before the Lutheran Assembly at Dixon, Ill., yesterday, Judge Grossecup, of the United States Circuit Court, said that government control of monopolies is essential to the perpetuation of American institutions.

A. E. Batson was hanged at Lake Charles, La., yesterday, for the murder of the Earl family in February, 1902, near Welsh. Batson always denied the crime. The board of pardons recommended his commutation, but Governor Heard disregarded the recommendation.

The Farmers and Merchants' Bank of Montgomery, Minn., was not opened for business yesterday, and the whereabouts of the cashier, B. A. Brainerd, is unknown. The deposits run from $50,000 to $60,000 and the liabilities are estimated at $150,000. No one knows what the assets amount to.

An examination of the condition of the City Trust and Banking Company, of Baltimore for which receivers were appointed last June, shows liabilities of $675,008 and estimated assets of $250,-468. This will wipe out the entire capital stock of $100,000 and leave a stockholders' liability of over $150,000.

The alleged embezzlement of $45,000 of the funds of the Commercial Banking Company, for which E. E. Johnson, the trusted clerk of the bank, is under arrest, has brought about the failure of the Merchants' Bank of Duluth, which closed its doors yesterday. This is the fourth bank suspending business as a result of the alleged embezzlement.

Sarah Polite, colored, and two children were killed by lightning Thursday at Brogdens, in Sunter county S. C. The woman was in the act of closing a window when killed. The infant in her arms was knocked across the room and seriously injured, but is still alive. The other two children were on the opposite side of the room.

Although promised protection by officials, negroes are continuing to leave Whitesboro, Texas, in large numbers, and it seems but a question of a short time until the city will be without a colored resident. The mob, which was foiled in an effort to lynch a negro Wednesday night, warned the negroes to leave and committed many depredations in the colored section. Several negroes were severely flogged, their houses entered and furniture destroyed.

The people of the Susquehanna river town of Wrightsville, Pa., are in a state of excitement due to the action of unknown negroes who chase and try to seize and assault unprotected white women on the streets at night. During the past several nights a dozen women have thus been thoroughly frightened by negroes. Citizens are planning to apprehend the offenders and, if successful, they threaten to deal out lynch law. The situation has caused race feeling to become strong among the whites of the town.

The accommodation passenger train from Pittsburg, on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, due at Wheeling, W. Va., at 1:30 yesterday evening, and a freight train met in a head-on collision near the Peninsula tunnel. The engine of the freight was almost completely demolished and the front of the passenger engine smashed in. Engineer Davis, of the freight, sustained a broken leg, while the two firemen had arms broken in the jump for safety. Several passengers were considerably shaken up and bruised, but were not otherwise injured.

Mrs. Perley G. Beach, of Parkersburg, W. Va., quarreled yesterday with Miss Louilla Cain, who, Mrs. Beach says, is the object of too marked attentions from Mr. Beach. Later Mrs. Beach met Miss Cain on the street and the latter drew a revolver, which she pressed against Mrs. Beach's breast and fired. Mrs. Beach pushed the pistol away and the ball took effect in her leg. She took the revolver away from Miss Cain, removed a knife which Miss Cain had in her belt and proceeded to give her a thrashing. Warrants are out for both women.

Prof. Charles Chollette, one of the most popular members of the faculty of the West Virginia University, was found dead about a mile from Morgantown, W. Va., yesterday morning. Professor Chollette had left home in the early morning to hunt squirrels, accompanied only by his dogs. In climbing over a fence with his gun cocked a rail had broken, throwing him over the fence on his gun with such force as to cause its discharge, the shot entering the abdomen on the lower left side and causing death from hemorrhages of the main blood vessel.

After arraying herself in evening dress for a dinner party, to which she had been invited last night, Mrs. Arthur E. Bradley, of New Haven, Conn., drank carbolic acid and died in the presence of her parents and family. Mrs. Bradley was the handsome daughter of Loren H. Stannard, a wealthy manufacturer of New Haven, and lived at his summer place, Woodmont, on the sound. Mrs. Bradley was unhappy in her married life. A short time ago she separated from her husband, who is a dealer in automobiles in Bridgeport and heir to an estate of $2,000,000. Since that time she had lived with her parents.

Citizens Threaten Lynching if Miscreants Are Apprehended.
YORK, Pa., Aug. 15.—The people of Wrightsville are in a state of excitement due to the action of unknown negroes who chase and try to seize and assault unprotected white women on the streets at night. Within the past several nights a dozen women have been thoroughly frightened by negroes.

Thursday night a negro pursued Lena Proff for several blocks and she was so overcome by fright that she was suffering severe nervous shock yesterday. Citizens are planning to apprehend the offenders and if successful they threaten to deal out lynch law.
